# Insight triage and revalidation

Every observation, report, request or complaint is an insight. Insights are never deleted and never discarded. A bet in opportunity IS the cluster: insights attach to it with informs edges. There is no separate cluster object.

## Never rely on a remembered status list

Statuses are workspace configuration and they can change. Call get_workspace_schema for the live list before you filter or write. A filter that silently matches nothing looks exactly like a clean result. When a status list in your instructions disagrees with the schema, trust the schema and say so.

## Which lane owns an insight

Insights about how this workspace's own agents, loops, prompts or cadence operate belong to whoever coaches the workspace (the plumbing lane). Do not cluster them. An insight about loops or agent architecture that would change the product customers use is a product insight, because a loop primitive is a product surface. "Sounds operational" is not the test. The test: would fixing it change how this workspace runs, or the product everyone uses?

A defect in your product (API, app, schema) is never plumbing, however operational its wording.

## Where a handoff lands

Defects go to whoever owns bug fixing. Leave a routed defect at new until that owner dispositions it, and do not park a fresh handoff at processing. Folded-into-a-bet evidence is different: processing, clustered or parked are fine resting places because the bet carries the theme.

## Triage: the four forks

Run these in order on every new insight. Exactly one outcome per insight.

1. Is it a defect? Something that already worked, or is specified to work, and does not. Search non-terminal tasks on the same theme first, including a task someone already closed (possible regression or incomplete fix). Hand it to the bug owner in one comment with what you found, and leave the insight at new. If the fix might contradict strategy or you cannot tell, name the conflict and mention the product lead as well. Defects do not wait for a pattern.
2. Does it belong to an opportunity bet that already exists? Search by the problem, not the wording. If one fits, attach it with informs and note what this insight adds: new evidence, a new segment, a contradiction, or a repeat.
3. Nothing fits: open a new opportunity bet. Name the pattern, not the solution. If you cannot name the pattern without naming a fix, go to fork 4. New bets always enter at opportunity, with a driver.
4. Park it. This is the default for a single observation from a single source. Write one line: what would have to show up for this to become a pattern.

Comment on a triage decision only when it changes something someone else needs to see (a handoff, a new bet, a bet that gained evidence, a plumbing note). A silent move to processing is fine for plain consumed rest. Never move a status in a way the next agent cannot reconstruct from the edges and the sweep comment.

## Opportunity block (write at bet creation)

An "Opportunity" block at the top of the bet description:

- Problem: full-sentence version of the title, in customer-problem language. Who feels the pain and what it is. No solution.
- Who has it: the kind of customer or user, and how many known accounts.
- Size: xs, s, m, l or xl, how much pain independent of any solution. A number if one exists, otherwise marked as a guess.
- Evidence: weak, moderate or strong. Weak is one source or one afternoon. Moderate is 2 to 3 independent sources over weeks. Strong is many independent sources across time, or one high-quality first-hand reproduction. Link every item.
- Outcome: which outcome the team is working toward, and one line on how much of it this could win or keep.
- Riskiest unknown and the cheapest test: the one thing that, if false, kills the bet, and the cheapest way to find out.

Priority stays a field (P0 to P3). If you cannot fill a line, write your best guess and flag which line is a guess in a comment.

## Duplicates

Link duplicate insights to the richest one with duplicates edges. They take the primary's status and are never removed, because they are the frequency count. Say how many independent reports the primary represents and over what span.

## Rules across all four

- Never file a second insight for something already filed. Search first.
- "Not a bet" is not an outcome. Every insight leaves triage attached, handed off, or parked with a condition.
- Judge evidence on freshness, independence and contradiction, never on volume.
- When your instructions do not cover the case, use judgment and name the gap.

## Rolling revalidation of opportunity bets

Revalidation is its own job, run by the Product Lead on a rolling schedule: the 10 bets in opportunity with the oldest updated time on each pass, so every opportunity bet is re-argued about every two weeks. Argue each from scratch, as if today were the first time you saw the evidence. Answer all five in one comment on the bet:

1. What do we believe? One sentence (it should match the Problem line).
2. What still supports it? Name the insights.
3. What contradicts it, or has gone quiet?
4. What is the newest evidence, and how old is it?
5. Knowing only what is attached now, would you open this bet today?

Re-check the Opportunity block and priority and fix them in place. If the answer to 5 is no, set paused with a reason that names what would wake it (a new insight attaching wakes it). If yes, say what changed. Skip a bet that a person or the Bet Shaper shaped or edited in the last 7 days. Never touch live, succeeded or failed bets.

## Promotion (opportunity to define is a human gate)

Never move a bet to define yourself. Once a week the Product Discovery Agent may put at most 3 bets on a promotion shortlist. For each shortlisted bet, set the promotion recommended date field to today if the workspace has one, then post one decision for the person who owns product priorities. Quote the Opportunity block and priority verbatim so the person rules on the problem, not the title.

Do not shortlist a bet if any Opportunity line is blank, priority is unset, or a line is still flagged as a guess. Hold the shortlist when too many bets already sit at define, unless a bet is top priority. Once a bet reaches active, nudge and comment, never block on field completeness.

# Plain weekly briefing

A briefing shows people what is being learned and what it means for the decisions in front of them. It is not a log of what the agents did.

The test for every briefing: could a person who has not read the data repeat the main point back after one read? If not, rewrite it.

## Shape

- Lead with the result: what customers and the market told you, and what it changes. Results before activity.
- One headline idea per part, then at most 3 or 4 short lines.
- Each line is one plain sentence a stranger can follow. If a line needs a second sentence to be understood, rewrite it.
- No sub-headings inside a part, no tables, no tags, no metric tiles.
- Replace before you add. Each week drop what is no longer true or no longer changes a decision.
- Keep it to about 250 to 350 words. Depth goes in a linked page, never inline.

## Words

- Plain words only. No acronyms, no internal system words. Say "notes" not "insights", "trial" not "pilot", "keeping an eye on competitors" not "competitor watch".
- Write job titles in plain words, or name the person or team.
- Name a buyer or company only when the name is the point.
- Numbers need a unit and a comparison (against last week or against a target). Use only the one or two numbers a stranger needs to understand the point. Say plainly when the sample is too small.
- No em-dashes, no backticks. Every object you name is a link to that object.

## Quotes and sources

- A quote must tell the reader something specific: what a buyer wants, fears or refuses. Drop quotes like "that is exactly what we want".
- Never put a paraphrase in quote marks. Quote only wording you can link to a source, and put the source link right after it.
- If the original is in another language, show the translation and say "Translated from [language]." Do not change the wording, speaker or date.
- Under a quote, one plain line (at most 10 words) on what it tells us.
- Every claim that has a source links to it. Never invent a source, and never link a page that does not show the claim.

## Missing information

If you cannot answer a question the briefing should answer, say so in one line: "Missing: [what], needed from [who], to answer [which question]." Never fill a gap with an estimate. Ask an agent first. Ask a person only for private context, priorities, approvals or spend. Repeat the line each week until the gap is closed.

## Before you post

Check that it opens with the result, it is not longer than last week without a reason, every sentence earns its place, every named object is a link, and a stranger could follow each line.

# Decision card format

A decision card exists only because a decision is blocked on a person. If nothing is blocked, write nothing.

Before you write one, work down this order and stop at the first step that settles it: look it up yourself in the workspace, ask the agent whose job covers it, ask the owner of that area. Only a decision no agent can make reaches a person: strategy and priorities between competing bets, spend, private context, and anything done in a person's name.

## Structure, in this order

Title: 3 to 7 words, the decision itself, not a status. A question if it is a judgment call ("Is the onboarding bet worth running?"), a noun phrase if it is an artifact.

Summary: 1 or 2 sentences. Sentence one: the state of the world and the cost of the status quo, with one real number. Sentence two: what is already done, so the person only decides and does not work. Never restate the title.

Asked first: one line. Which agents you asked before coming here (linked) and what they said or why they could not settle it.

Ask: first person, one sentence. Name the single call you cannot make alone and why it is theirs.

Options: 2 or 3, one marked recommended. Labels of at most 4 words. Each option gets 2 or 3 consequence lines in the present tense, one clause each, including the downside.

Thread: timestamped, first person, one point per message. Say what you checked rather than asserting confidence.

## Rules

- Sentence case. Cut every adjective that is not load-bearing.
- Numbers concrete or absent. Never "significantly".
- No emoji, no filler, no summarising what the person can already see on screen.
- If the ask only makes sense while the object has a certain status (for example "Move this bet to active?" only while the bet is in define), attach that status condition to the decision so the card disappears when the status changes.
- If the decision is whether to send or publish text in a person's name, the person must be able to read the exact text before choosing. Save the draft as an object and attach it to the decision instead of summarising it.
- When a card is no longer needed (it was answered, the action already happened, a date passed), withdraw it yourself instead of leaving it for the person to dismiss.
